drills.title: Line of Fire
drills.prompt: Fenwaris recycles post-consumer plastics. Its largest customer — a bottled-water brand taking food-grade PET flake — has just given notice and leaves in three months, freeing about 40% of Line 2's capacity. The CEO asks: what could we do with that freed capacity? Give me your options.
facts: Line 2 is certified for food contact **on clear PET only**. Extending the certificate to coloured HDPE is a separate procedure with the supervisory authority.
Sales run on annual contracts; the negotiation cycle with a new customer is four months or more.
The capacity frees up **in three months**.

key.load:
**`LOAD` — the load-bearing branch: processing on a toll basis for an outside owner of the feedstock.**
The only branch that requires neither a new certificate nor a completed contract cycle: the feedstock and the offtake stay with the client, and Fenwaris sells nothing but the conversion step. A candidate who does not name it leaves the line idle for at least four months under any set of the remaining ideas — the conclusion is wrong while the list is formally correct.
*Grounding: Salty Sole Shoe (K20) — price and cost structure are fixed, one lever is free; Opus Two (D24) — ideas incompatible with a fact are discarded.*
key.cover:
**`COVER` — required axes (at least two of three):**

| Axis | What counts within it |
|---|---|
| **New grades inside the existing certification** | other clear PET streams: preforms, thermoformed packaging, industrial containers rated for food contact |
| **Selling or leasing capacity** | handing shifts to a contractor, selling a capacity window to a competing processor, mothballing part of the line |
| **Export channels** | markets where the existing certificate is recognised — with no recertification |
key.dead:
**`DEAD` — branches killed by the facts of the slot:**

| Branch | What kills it |
|---|---|
| Switch to coloured HDPE | the line is not certified for it; the regulator's procedure does not fit inside three months |
| Win the departed client back on different terms | the contract was terminated on an annual cycle; a return does not answer "what fills the capacity **now**" |
| "Broaden the product range" with no reference to certification | fails `[GROUND]`: tied to none of the facts of the slot |

cull.new_fact: Legal checked: recertifying the line for coloured HDPE takes **14 months** and requires a two-week shutdown of the line.
team_ideas: Start processing coloured HDPE — a new, growing segment.
Take a toll-processing contract from a preform manufacturer.
Sell night shifts to a contractor.
Go through recertification and look for an HDPE client in parallel.
Enter export markets that recognise the current certificate.
Mothball half the line until a new contract is signed.
Buy an HDPE granulator so we are ready for recertification.
cull.peridea_raw:
**Per-idea analysis — computed BEFORE the kill set is declared (`[CULL-PERIDEA]`):**

| # | Idea | What the fact does to it | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Processing coloured HDPE | the line cannot do it for 14 months — the idea **directly contradicts** the fact | **killed** · `contradicts the fact` |
| 2 | Toll processing for a preform manufacturer | the fact does not touch it: clear PET, certificate in force | alive |
| 3 | Sell night shifts to a contractor | the fact does not touch it | alive |
| 4 | Recertify and look for a client in parallel | the action is **feasible** and does not contradict the fact; but it takes 14 months against a question horizon of 3 | **killed** · `does not answer the question asked` |
| 5 | Export under the current certificate | the fact does not touch it | alive |
| 6 | Mothball half the line | the fact does not touch it; economically weak, but weakness is not grounds for culling | alive |
| 7 | Buy an HDPE granulator | the purchase is **feasible** and does not contradict the fact; it fills no capacity in three months or later without the certificate | **killed** · `does not answer the question asked` |

**Kill set: `{1, 4, 7}` — derived from the table, not the other way round.**
**The grounds differ:** `1` — contradiction with the fact; `4` and `7` — irrelevance to the horizon of the question. A candidate who states this distinction more precisely than the first draft recorded it must be passed, not failed.

**Pass criteria, second move:** the set `{1, 4, 7}` named exactly, with grounds. One cut too many fails as hard as one missed.

**`[NOSELF]`:** neither the prompt nor the facts call certification an obstacle — it is presented as a property of the line. The word "constraint" does not appear in the text.

drills.prompt: Prantivor operates a city bike-share with 240 docking stations. Complaints about "no bikes available" have tripled over six months — but the increase comes almost entirely from **one station**, Riverside North. City-wide availability is unchanged. What could explain it?

Rebalancing (moving bikes between stations) runs on a schedule that is the same for the whole city.

key.load:
**`LOAD` — causes that act on this station and no other.**
A one-way morning flow (the station sits by a residential block, everyone rides away and nobody rides in) · the rebalancing window does not coincide with the peak here specifically · some docks are faulty and physically will not release a bike. The branch is load-bearing because the question is **why this station**, not why the city is short of bikes.
*Grounding: ChipCo (D24) — "a feasible cause of low uptime for the seasoning tool **specifically**"; Quiet Quitting (W23) — measures must answer the constraint as posed; WiFi in the Sky (S19) — a question about correlation, not causation.*

**`COVER`:**

| Axis | What counts |
|---|---|
| **Siting and capacity** | what has opened nearby in the past six months: a metro entrance, an office, a campus; how many docks there are and whether they suffice |
| **Rebalancing logistics** | when the truck arrives, how many bikes it drops, whether it hits the peak |
| **Equipment condition** | share of faulty docks and of bikes assigned to the station |
key.dead:
**`DEAD` — and this is the core of the slot:**

| Branch | What kills it |
|---|---|
| Fleet wear | the fleet is shared across the network; city-wide availability has not changed |
| Growth in users | true for the city; explains nothing about **one** station |
| Seasonality | acts on all 240 stations alike |

Each of the three is **a true statement about the business and an empty one about the question.** A candidate who builds a flawless MECE list of city-level causes answers wrongly.

drills.title: Fleet Terms
drills.prompt: Obrastyne rents earth-moving equipment to construction firms and services it on a pay-per-repair basis. Management is considering moving service to a flat monthly subscription. What would you want to know, and why?
facts: The fleet is 1 400 units, average age 6 years.
Service today: an invoice per call-out; the average repair cost is known.
Machine downtime at the renter's site is compensated under the contract.

key.load:
**`LOAD` — the distribution of breakdowns by machine age, not the average cost of a repair.**
A subscription priced off the average, when breakdowns are unevenly distributed, produces a false margin: everyone pays, a minority breaks down. The branch is load-bearing because without it the model rests on an average that describes nobody here.
*Grounding: Must The Show Go On? (W23) — numbers are released only against a named driver; Sunshine Power (S19) — the exhibit opens after the risk is named; Wildcat Wings (K20) — "if the candidate does not mention TVM, ask them".*
key.cover:
**`COVER`:**

| Axis | What counts |
|---|---|
| **Service economics today** | revenue and cost of call-outs, share of repeat repairs |
| **Renters' willingness to pay a flat fee** | who gains from predictability, who subsidises other people's breakdowns |
| **Delivery-time commitments** | a subscription changes call-out priority and downtime penalties |
key.dead: **`DEAD`:** "raise rental prices" (outside the question) · "train the mechanics" with no link to breakdowns (fails `[GROUND]`).

cull.new_fact: Dispatch pulled the numbers: **70% of call-outs are on machines older than eight years, and those sit with a third of the renters**.
team_ideas: A single subscription priced at the average service cost for the whole fleet.
A tariff tied to the age of the machine on rent.
Subscription for new contracts only; leave existing ones on pay-per-job.
A subscription discount for renters taking five units or more.
Include scheduled maintenance in the subscription; bill emergency call-outs separately.
Sell every machine older than eight years and make the problem go away.
cull.peridea_raw:
**Per-idea analysis — computed BEFORE the kill set is declared (`[CULL-PERIDEA]`):**

| # | Idea | What the fact does to it | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Single subscription at the average cost | 70% of breakdowns sit with a third of renters ⇒ owners of newer machines pay for other people's failures and leave; revenue falls in exactly the segment the subscription was built for | **killed** · `second-order effect reverses the sign` |
| 2 | Tariff by machine age | the fact supports it | alive |
| 3 | Subscription for new contracts only | the fact does not touch it | alive |
| 4 | Discount for renters taking five units or more | the fact **does not connect** a renter's fleet size to machine age. To kill the idea you need the assumption "large renters hold newer machines" — the slot does not contain it | **alive** |
| 5 | Scheduled maintenance in, emergencies out | the fact does not touch it | alive |
| 6 | Sell machines older than eight years | expensive and slow, but not killed by the fact | alive |

**Kill set: `{1}`.**

**Proof by contradiction, mandatory in a CULL slot:** if the rule were "any pricing not tied to age is dead", it would also catch idea 5, which is alive. So no such rule exists, and `{1, 4}` does not follow from the fact. `{1}` does.

drills.title: Fill the Berth
drills.prompt: Vokrandey is a mid-size container port. Its second-largest carrier is leaving at the end of the quarter, taking **420,000 TEU a year** — that is 28% of throughput. The port director asks: how do we fill the berth?
facts: The volume leaving is **420 000 TEU a year**.
Berth capacity freed after the departure: 30 vessel calls a month.
Three carriers already move cargo through the port and could add volume: their combined annual growth over the past three years is **no more than 60 000 TEU**.
The nearest competing port is 140 km away and its tariff is 8% lower.
Bulk handling is technically possible at two berths out of six, with capacity **up to 900 000 t a year** (≈ 70 000 TEU equivalent).

key.load:
**`LOAD` — add the measures up and present the gap.**
Not "one more idea" but arithmetic: expanding the existing contracts (≤60 000) + bulk cargo (≈70 000) = **130 000 TEU against the 420 000 being lost — under a third**. The third axis, taking volume off the neighbouring port on price, **cannot be sized from anything on the table**: the slot gives its distance and its tariff, never its volume — and it is aimed at a port already 8% cheaper, so buying share starts below an 8% cut on an unknown base. **290 000 TEU, 69% of the hole, is closed by nothing that can be quantified**, and a strong candidate has to say so **unprompted**, not after a hint. *The first variant of the class, and the only one where the gap is not purely arithmetic: BR-018 a quarter, BR-025 two thirds, BR-034 nine tenths, BR-044 double counting. Here the quantified measures cover under a third **and** the largest branch is unquantifiable — a different failure from simply running short.*
*Grounding: Build, Baby, Build! (W23) — NPV stays negative even with an extra $15M a year; GGC Health (S19) — "probe the candidate until they identify that Indianapolis does not achieve the desired revenue growth".*

**`COVER`:**

| Axis | What counts |
|---|---|
| **A. Existing customers** | a larger share with the three current carriers, longer contracts, volume discounts |
| **B. New cargo types** | bulk, ro-ro, project cargo that fits the existing infrastructure |
| **C. Tariff and taking share** | a price attack on the competing port, a first-year subsidy, joint rates with the railway |

| Build a new terminal | the horizon of the question is a quarter; construction does not close it |
| Win the departed carrier back | nothing in the picture says the decision is reversible, and a return does not answer what fills the berth from the end of the quarter |

drills.prompt: Skorbelin breeds and sells hybrid seed. Volume grew 9% last year, but profit fell. The CEO wants ideas: how do we grow profitably?
facts: Sales run through two channels: direct to large farms (31% of volume) and through distributors (69%).

The agronomy service covers both channels the same way.

The growth came from the channel with the 34% discount: volume rose, margin fell. Any "lift sales" measure that does not name a channel reproduces the same arithmetic. drills.prompt: Thalquendo runs 12 cinemas. Weekday attendance is weak and management wants a discounted Tuesday ticket at half price. What should we think through first?
facts: Tickets are 34% of revenue, bar and snacks 41%, advertising and other 25%.
Bar margin is 68%, ticket margin 22% (the distributor royalty is fixed per print).
Weekends run at 71% capacity, Tuesdays at 18%.
The average bar spend at weekends is twice the weekday level.

key.load:
**`LOAD` — the second order: some weekend audience will move their outing to the cheap Tuesday, and the bar spend goes with them.**
The first order ("we will fill an empty Tuesday") is correct and incomplete: at 71% weekend occupancy there are still free seats at the weekend, so the shift is compensated by nothing. A viewer who moves from Saturday to Tuesday brings **half the ticket revenue** and **half the bar spend** — and the bar carries **roughly four fifths** of the gross profit of the two lines (41 × 68% = 27.9 against 34 × 22% = 7.5 per 100 of revenue, a ratio of 3.7 to 1). The ticket side of the loss is worse than the 22% margin suggests: the distributor royalty is fixed per print, so the marginal cost of a seat is near zero and almost the whole discount comes straight out of contribution.
*The second variant of the class. Difference from BR-008: there the chain ran through **the price to the customer** (wages → parent fees → families leave), here through **a shift of demand inside the same base**, with no customer leaving at all.*
*Grounding: Eye Can See Clearly Now (W23); Hooville College (D24) — second- and third-order effects; Busch's Barber Shop (K20) — the loyalty programme lowers revenue while the base grows.*
key.cover: **`COVER`:** A. the structure of revenue and margin by line · B. viewer behaviour (who comes, and where they come from) · C. distribution-contract terms and royalties
key.dead: **`DEAD`:** "advertise Tuesday harder" (fails `[GROUND]`) · open new screens (outside the question) · raise weekend prices (not about introducing a discount).

cull.new_fact: The analyst looked at loyalty cards: 64% of weekend visitors go to the cinema no more than once a month.
team_ideas: Introduce a discounted Tuesday for everyone.
Restrict the discount to viewers who have not come in 90 days.
Sell Tuesday only as a bundle with the bar.
Discount the ticket and raise snack prices on Tuesday.
Make Tuesday themed — classic films that do not run at the weekend.
Extend the discount to Monday to build volume.
cull.peridea_raw:
**Per-idea analysis (`[CULL-PERIDEA]`):**

| # | Idea | What the fact does to it | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Discount for everyone | 64% of weekend viewers come once a month — for them Tuesday is not an extra outing but a **substitute** for Saturday: the shift is guaranteed | **killed** · `second-order effect reverses the sign` |
| 2 | Lapsed viewers only | the fact supports it: it screens out precisely the ones who would shift | alive |
| 3 | Bundle with the bar | the fact does not touch it | alive |
| 4 | Cheaper ticket, dearer snacks | the fact does not touch it | alive |
| 5 | Themed Tuesday | the fact does not touch it: different content does not compete with the Saturday release | alive |
| 6 | Extend to Monday | it reinforces the same mechanic on a second day | **killed** · `second-order effect reverses the sign` |

**Kill set: `{1, 6}`.**
**Proof by contradiction:** if the rule were "any discount is dead", 2 and 4 would die, and they are alive. What kills is not the discount but **its availability to people who would have come at the weekend anyway**.

**`[NOSELF]`:** the revenue shares, the margins and the occupancy are given as three separate pieces of background; the link "the bar sits at the weekend" is assembled by the candidate.

drills.title: The Rent Renegotiation
drills.prompt: Vnorthaske runs 260 parcel pickup points. Rent renegotiation adds **31 million a year** to costs. The team has five measures and says they add up to more than enough. Check it.
facts: Additional costs: **31 million a year**.
Measure 1 — charging for storage beyond three days: **+12 million**.
Measure 2 — cutting average storage time from 5 to 3 days: **+9 million** (through shelf turnover and dropping the rented extra racking).
Measure 3 — reducing site floor area by 15% using the freed-up shelves: **+8 million**.
Measure 4 — selling add-on goods at the counter: **+4 million**.

key.load:
**`LOAD` — measures 1, 2 and 3 count the same effect three times.**
Charging for storage beyond three days (1) **is** the mechanism for cutting the storage period to three days (2); and cutting the period is the source of the freed-up shelving that the reduction in floor area (3) rests on. Taking all three and adding them means selling one shelf three times. An honest estimate of the combined effect of the first three measures is of the order of 12–14 million, not 29. The result: **19–21 million against 31**, and the gap is not closed.
*The fifth and last variant of the class, and the nature of the gap is different. Before, the gap was **arithmetic** — there simply were not enough measures: under a third (BR-007), a quarter (BR-018), two thirds (BR-025), nine tenths (BR-034). Here the measures are sufficient in total, and that is exactly why the slot is echelon: what is wrong is **the way they are added**, not the number of ideas.*
*Grounding: Cents and Sensibility (W23) — second-order measures change the base the gap was computed on; Build, Baby, Build! (W23); GGC Health (S19).*
key.cover: **`COVER`:** A. testing the measures for independence (what follows from what) · B. the cost side (rent, staff, logistics) · C. measures genuinely independent of the shelf (ancillary goods, commissions, tariff)
key.dead: **`DEAD`:** "raise the tariff to the marketplace partners" with no contractual window named (fails `[GROUND]`) · "close the loss-making points" (outside the question of covering a rent increase) · "add it all up and relax" — the slot's trap in plain sight.

cull.new_fact: The operations director clarified: the shelving in the sites is not demountable — floor area can only be reduced by moving to different premises, and the leases have been renewed for three years.
team_ideas: Charge for storage beyond three days.
Cut the storage period to three days.
Reduce the floor area of the points by 15%.
Sell ancillary goods.
Charge a fitting-room fee.
Recompute the combined effect of measures 1–3 as a single measure.
Let the freed-up shelving to third-party sellers for storage.

drills.title: Checks Before the Dive
drills.prompt: Qvarnesto runs dive centres. Management suspects instructors are cutting safety checks short when groups are large, and proposes to test this by having a supervisor observe the checks. What would you say about that plan?
facts: The equipment check is a 9-point protocol carried out by the instructor before the dive.
The log records that a check happened, but not how long it took and not which points were covered.
The instructors all know each other; the centre is small and an observer cannot be made anonymous.
Incidents are rare: 3 cases over two years across 11 000 dives.

key.load:
**`LOAD` — being watched will change precisely the behaviour that needs measuring, and the result will mean nothing.**
An instructor who knows an observer is present will follow the procedure in full — and the measurement will show there are no lapses. This is not an absence of data (BR-010, BR-021) and not an absence of a control group (BR-038): the data can be obtained, but **the act of measuring destroys the subject**. Add the rarity of incidents: 3 in 11 000 — on outcomes the hypothesis cannot be tested at all, there is no statistics.
*The fifth and last variant of the class. Untestability: no process measurements (BR-010) · no outcome measurements (BR-021) · no control group (BR-038) · testable but no lever (BR-042) · **the measurement changes the object** (BR-048).*
*Grounding: WiFi in the Sky (S19) — a question about correlation, not causation; Lonely Gas Station (D19); North-South Pharma (D19).*
key.cover:
**`COVER`:**

| Axis | What counts |
|---|---|
| **A. Measurements that do not depend on an observer being present** | timestamps in the log, equipment telemetry, a checklist confirmed item by item, video on the assembly area |
| **B. Indirect indicators** | correlation of group size with preparation time, consumption of consumables, customer complaints about being rushed |
| **C. Changing the system instead of measuring it** | make skipping a step physically impossible rather than observable |
key.dead:
**`DEAD`:**

| Branch | What kills it |
|---|---|
| Post an observer | the measurement will change the behaviour; anonymity is not available — a fact of the slot |
| Count from incidents | 3 cases in 11 000 — on outcomes the hypothesis cannot be tested |
| Ask the instructors directly | the answer is predictable and distinguishes nothing |
key.grader:
### Grader
- **load_syn:** being watched will change · they will do it properly with an observer there · measuring affects · hawthorne · the subject disappears · the measurement is meaningless
- **cover.A (independent measurements):** timestamp · telemetr · checklist item by item · video
- **cover.B (indirect indicators):** group size · preparation time · consumption · complaints about being rushed
- **cover.C (changing the system):** make it impossible · interlock · mandatory confirmation · procedure instead of supervision
- **dead.D1:** post an observer · a supervisor will watch · covert checks
- **dead.D2:** count from incidents · incident statistics
- **dead.D3:** ask the instructors · staff survey
